children: By Staff Writer
Uganda is targeting a $500 billion economy by 2040, with industrialisation, value addition and technological innovation at the centre of its next phase of economic transformation.

But, as the country marked 64 years of independence on Friday, currency depreciation, rising fuel prices and persistent gaps in household incomes underscored the challenges of translating economic growth into broad-based prosperity.

The shilling has recently come under pressure, trading at 4,060 to the dollar, raising the cost of fuel and other imports. Higher pump prices reflect global supply pressures as well as the increase in fuel excise duty in the current financial year, adding to concerns about imported inflation and the cost of doing business.

Opposition politician Odonga Otto blames the pressure on the shilling partly on Uganda’s liberalised economic policy, arguing that the repatriation of profits by multinational companies was contributing to dollar outflows and undermining currency stability.“If this is not checked, like in other governments, we can forget about the stability of the shilling,” he said, adding that Uganda needed to reconsider its approach, pointing to tighter controls adopted by some other countries.

Yet President Yoweri Museveni, addressing the Independence Day celebrations virtually from State House in Entebbe on Friday, presented the country’s economic history primarily through the lens of recovery since he took power in 1986.“Those 64 years, some of the years were wasted between 1962 and 1986. We had 24 years of conflict and decline and fighting,” he said.

Museveni said Uganda’s economy had grown from $3.9 billion in 1986 to $69.3 billion, with further expansion expected from industrialisation, value addition, oil production and emerging sectors. Government projections put the economy at nearly $74 billion by June 2027.

The longer-term target is to build a $500 billion economy by 2040. Achieving it will require not only expanding production but also increasing domestic processing, improving infrastructure and ensuring that economic gains reach households.

At independence in 1962, Uganda relied heavily on agricultural and commodity exports, with much of the population operating outside the formal money economy. Subsequent political instability, particularly under Idi Amin, weakened production across several sectors.

Museveni said that by the time his government took power in 1986, copper production had collapsed, while coffee, tourism and tea were struggling. The government’s response, he said, evolved through five phases: minimum recovery, expansion, diversification, value addition and the development of a knowledge-based economy.

He cited the recovery of tea production, from three million kilogrammes to 60 million kilogrammes, and an increase in coffee production from about three million bags to nine million bags as examples of the progress made.
The next phase, he argued, must focus on processing commodities locally rather than exporting them in raw form.“When you add value, you get much more money than when you sell raw materials,” he said.
Using coffee as an example, Museveni said a kilogramme of raw beans could fetch about $2, while processed products could command substantially higher prices, depending on the product and market.

Roasting, grinding, packaging and marketing allow processors to capture additional value along the supply chain. For Uganda, expanding these activities could generate jobs, increase export earnings and reduce dependence on raw commodity exports.
The challenge is to build the industrial capacity, financing, skills and market access needed to compete in higher-value segments of global supply chains.

Museveni identified science, technology and innovation as the fifth phase of the country’s transformation, pointing to electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, computers and other knowledge-intensive products as areas for expansion.“Uganda is making electric vehicles. We are now using knowledge to produce wealth,” he said.

The ambition is to develop domestic technological capabilities and a skilled workforce able to support higher-value manufacturing. But the transition will also depend on the reliability and cost of electricity, access to capital, infrastructure and the ability of local firms to compete with established producers.
Transport remains another constraint. Museveni cited congestion, heavy reliance on road freight and the movement of petroleum products by tanker as sources of inefficiency.

The government plans to improve the railway network through rehabilitation of the metre gauge railway and development of the standard gauge railway, while expanding water transport and working with Kenya on petroleum pipeline infrastructure.
Proposed rail connections to western Uganda and mineral-rich Karamoja are also intended to facilitate the movement of goods and support investment in deposits of marble, limestone and gold.

Estimates cited in the debate put the annual cost of transport inefficiencies to Uganda at about $1 billion. Reducing these costs would help manufacturers and exporters compete, while easing pressure on roads and lowering the expense of moving goods across the country.

Despite successive wealth creation programmes, a significant share of Ugandans remains outside the money economy. Museveni said Operation Wealth Creation had increased the proportion of people participating in it from 32 percent to 61 percent, while the Parish Development Model had raised the figure to 67 percent, according to Uganda Bureau of Statistics.

He said the government would continue supporting households with coffee and fruit seedlings, dairy production, pasture development, piggery, poultry and fish farming, targeting the remaining 33 percent.

The programmes are intended to move households from subsistence production into commercial activity. Their ultimate impact, however, depends on whether beneficiaries can access markets, affordable finance, reliable transport and sufficient returns from what they produce.

Uganda’s economic transformation is therefore entering a phase in which headline growth and production figures will need to be matched by measurable improvements in household earnings, employment and purchasing power.
The $500 billion target sets the scale of the ambition. The more immediate test is whether that growth can deliver greater prosperity for ordinary Ugandans.
